# Evidence for the diagrams: inspect the closure cells directly
broken = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print("broken results:", [f() for f in broken])
print("one shared box?",
      broken[0].__closure__[0] is broken[1].__closure__[0] is broken[2].__closure__[0])

def make_fn(i):
    return lambda: i

fixed = [make_fn(i) for i in range(3)]
print("\nfixed results:", [f() for f in fixed])
print("distinct boxes?",
      fixed[0].__closure__[0] is not fixed[1].__closure__[0])
print("each box's contents:", [f.__closure__[0].cell_contents for f in fixed])

# Fix 1 (default argument) is different again: no closure at all
fix1 = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
print("\nfix1 results:", [f() for f in fix1])
print("fix1 closures:", [f.__closure__ for f in fix1])   # [None, None, None]
description: A list comprehension builds all lambdas in one scope so they share one binding. A factory call creates a fresh scope per lambda so each captures its own.

steps.description: broken builds three lambdas in one comprehension scope. They all capture the same i.
make_fn takes i and returns a lambda that captures i from its own call's scope.
fixed builds each lambda in a separate call to make_fn, giving each its own i.

steps.description: fix1 uses a default argument i=i to bind i at definition time, so no closure is needed.

Running prints broken results: [2, 2, 2], one shared box? True, fixed results: [0, 1, 2], distinct boxes? True, each box's contents: [0, 1, 2], fix1 results: [0, 1, 2], and fix1 closures: [None, None, None].

title: The Loop Trap: One Shared Box vs Three Distinct Boxes
